Breaking Shame: Confession, Forgiveness and the Exit from Babylon

The questions this study answers: (1) If I already know my I Am Nots and know the gospel truth, why does shame still have to be broken? (2) How does the gospel actually heal shame? (3) Why does confession matter, toward God and toward people? (4) Why does confession dismantle the Babylonian system? (5) Does God forgive only when we confess? Is confession a tool? (6) Where do Kruger, Jesudian, and Joshua James Roberts emphasize different things about breaking shame, vulnerability, and heart healing?

Source note (please read). I researched all three teachers before writing. Baxter Kruger is well documented: Trinitarian, relational theology; the Father's dream of including us in the life of the Trinity; and the framework used through this whole series (I Am Nots, the fallen mind, self-salvation and escape). Jesudian Silvester pastors The Father's House in Chennai; his church publicly describes its focus as God's unconditional love and sonship, and his ministry lists practicing vulnerability to facilitate belonging, combating shame, fear and anxiety, and holding stories as holy ground. A sermon of his titled "Confession that heals" exists, but I could only see its title, not its content. Joshua James Roberts: I could not find reliable public material under that name, so I have not attributed any specific teaching to him. Part 7 sets out the real fault lines on this topic and leaves a structured place for you to add what he actually teaches from your notes or transcripts. Where this document speaks about their "clash," that is my analysis of how these emphases can pull against each other, not a claim about what any of them said about each other.

PART 1: Why Shame Must Be Broken Even When We Know the I Am Nots

1.1 Knowing the lie is not the same as being free of it

In earlier studies we named the I Am Nots (not good enough, not included, not worthy, not adopted, and so on), traced where they came from, and matched each with the gospel's "I Am." That work is essential, but it operates mainly at the level of understanding. Shame does not live only in understanding. It lives in the body (the flinch, the hot face, the urge to hide), in memory, in the nervous system, and above all in relationship, because shame was learned in relationship: a look, a tone, a silence, a comparison.

LevelWhat it doesWhat it cannot do alone
Insight (I know my I Am Not)Names the lie, breaks its invisibilityDoes not change the body's alarm response or the fear of being seen
Truth (I know what the gospel says)Supplies the true identity to replace the lieTruth in the head can coexist with shame in the gut for years
Experience (I am seen and received)Gives the nervous system evidence that exposure is survivableNeeds safe relationship to happen; cannot be self-generated

Shame is a wound that happened in relationship, so its healing has to be relational. You can identify a lie privately. You cannot be accepted privately. That is why knowing your I Am Nots is the beginning of freedom, not the end.

1.2 What shame does: the hiding cycle

Shame says: "I AM bad / not enough" (identity, not behavior)
↓
Exposure feels deadly (to be seen = to be rejected)
↓
Hide: fig leaves, performance, image management, silence, numbing
↓
Hiding prevents the very acceptance that would disprove the lie
↓
Lie is never tested, so it stays in charge; isolation deepens

This is Genesis 3 in miniature. Adam and Eve's first response to shame was not to sin more but to cover and hide (Gen 3:7–10): "I was afraid because I was naked, so I hid." Kruger's two fallen strategies map exactly: self-salvation (fig leaves: performance, control, looking right) and escape (hiding in the trees: avoidance, numbing, withdrawal). Shame will keep running both strategies until it is brought into the light and met with acceptance.

1.3 Why unbroken shame quietly damages everything

DomainHow unbroken shame shows upLink to earlier studies
RelationshipsCannot receive love; sabotages closeness; the wallHardened Hearts study
Spiritual lifeKeeps God at arm's length; treats Him as an evaluatorFallen Mind; Saved to Wholeness
Body and mindAnxiety, rumination, procrastination, OCD-type cyclesEmotional-Neurological Framework
CharacterPerfectionism or self-sabotage becomes identityBelief and Character Formation
Vulnerability to controlShame-driven people are easiest to manipulate and exploitExploitation and Disguised Control

PART 2: How the Gospel Heals Shame

2.1 The direction of movement reverses

In Genesis 3 humanity hides from God. In the gospel God comes to the hiding. The pattern of Scripture is a Father who seeks, covers, and welcomes before anything is cleaned up.

MomentWhat God does with shame
Genesis 3:9, 21Calls "Where are you?" (a question of love, not detection) and clothes them Himself
Isaiah 54:4; 61:7Promises no more shame; double honor in its place
John 4Meets a woman avoiding the village at noon; knows everything and stays at the well
John 8:1–11Stands between the exposed woman and her accusers: "Neither do I condemn you"
Luke 15:20–24Runs, embraces, robes, rings, feasts, all before the son's speech is finished
Hebrews 12:2Jesus "despised the shame": He took the naked, exposed, mocked position on the cross
Romans 8:1; 10:11No condemnation; whoever believes in Him will not be put to shame

2.2 The Trinitarian answer

Kruger's central insight is that shame's core question, "Am I acceptable?", was answered before we asked it. In Christ, humanity is included in the Father's love for the Son through the Spirit. Shame's verdict ("you are outside, unwanted") is not merely comforted; it is overruled by a prior fact. The Father's response to the fallen mind is not to demand a fix but to enter the far country in the Son and bring us home. So the gospel heals shame by (1) declaring a new identity, (2) demonstrating it in a Person who carried our exposure, and (3) inviting us into a lived experience of that acceptance, which is where confession, community, and vulnerability come in.

Truth declared, truth demonstrated, truth experienced. The third is where many of us stall. We can affirm "I am accepted" and still live hidden. Confession is one of the God-given ways the third movement becomes real.

PART 3: What Confession Is (and Is Not)

3.1 The meaning

The New Testament word behind "confess" (homologeo) means to "say the same thing," to agree. Confession is agreeing with God about reality: what happened, what it did, and what He says about me now. It is bringing what was hidden into the light where the Father already stands. It is not informing God (He knows), not paying a fee, and not self-punishment.

PassageWhat it shows about confession
Psalm 32:3–5Silence made "my bones waste away"; acknowledging brought relief and forgiveness. Hiding hurts the hider.
Proverbs 28:13Concealing does not prosper; confessing and turning finds mercy.
1 John 1:5–9Walking in the light brings fellowship and cleansing; confession is agreeing with the light.
James 5:16Confess to one another and pray for one another so that you may be healed. The stated goal is healing, not punishment.
Romans 2:4God's kindness leads to repentance; kindness is the atmosphere confession grows in.
2 Corinthians 7:10Godly grief leads to life; worldly sorrow (shame spiral) leads to death.

3.2 Two directions: vertical and horizontal

Toward God (vertical)Toward safe people (horizontal)
What it accomplishesEnds the hiding posture with Him; the conscience receives what Christ already did; fellowship is felt againBreaks isolation; another human face responds with acceptance, giving the nervous system real evidence (mirror-neuron and attachment healing)
What it healsGuilt, sense of distance from GodShame, aloneness, "if they knew, they'd leave"
Why both are neededShame was learned with people and God is often experienced through people. Vertical alone can leave the relational wound intact; horizontal alone can lack the ultimate foundation. James 5:16 and 1 John 1:9 stand side by side for a reason.

3.3 What confession is NOT

  • Not a payment. It does not purchase forgiveness or a better standing.
  • Not self-flagellation. Endless self-condemnation is shame dressed as piety.
  • Not public exposure of everything to everyone. Wisdom chooses safe, mature listeners.
  • Not coerced. Forced or performed confession, especially demanded by a leader, is control, not healing (see Part 6.3).
  • Not required for things done to you. Being abused, betrayed, or shamed is not a sin to confess. See Part 9.3.

PART 4: Does God Only Forgive When We Confess? Is Confession a Tool?

This is a genuine point of disagreement among sincere Christians, so it is worth laying out the positions fairly before giving the relational-gospel reading.

4.1 Two ways Christians read it

View A: Forgiveness is applied when we confessView B: Forgiveness is already given in Christ; confession is how we receive and live in it
Key texts1 John 1:9 ("if we confess... He is faithful and just to forgive"); Acts 3:19; Luke 24:47; Matthew 6:12Colossians 2:13–14 (forgave all our trespasses); 2 Corinthians 5:19 (not counting their trespasses against them); Ephesians 4:32; Romans 5:8; Hebrews 10:10–14
EmphasisPersonal, ongoing repentance keeps relationship clear; unconfessed sin blocks fellowshipForgiveness is a finished act at the cross; the human role is to awaken to it and stop hiding
Risk if overstatedGod's love becomes conditional on our accurate, complete confession (anxious "did I confess everything?" living)Confession is treated as unnecessary, leaving hidden shame and unhealed relationships untouched

4.2 The relational-gospel reading (consistent with Kruger's framework)

God's forgiveness does not begin when we confess. It begins in Christ, before we were asking (Rom 5:8). But our experience of that forgiveness, our fellowship, and our healing do involve us, and confession is the doorway we walk through. A gift already given still has to be received to be enjoyed.

The Luke 15 test. The younger son rehearses a confession speech ("Father, I have sinned... make me like one of your hired servants"). But the father sees him a long way off, runs, embraces, and kisses him before he speaks (v. 20). When the son begins his speech, the father cuts off the "hired servant" part and calls for the robe and ring (vv. 21–22). The father's acceptance did not wait for the confession. Yet the son did come home, did speak, did receive. Confession was real, but it was the son's way of entering what the father had already prepared, not the father's condition for loving him.

4.3 Confession as a tool, not a currency

Confession as CURRENCY (Babylonian)Confession as TOOL (Kingdom)
"Say it right so God will forgive me""Say it truly so I can stop hiding and receive what's already mine"
Purpose: change God's attitude toward mePurpose: change my posture (fear → trust) and my relationships
Produces anxiety, scrupulosity, performanceProduces relief, closeness, freedom
Treats God as a judge to be satisfiedTreats God as a Father to be trusted
Endless (never sure it counted)Complete (say it, receive it, walk on)

Think of a doctor's office. The cure is real and available, but you still have to walk in and show where it hurts. The doctor's willingness to heal does not depend on your speech; your healing does involve your showing up.

PART 5: How Confession Actually Breaks Shame

5.1 The psychological mechanism

Shame's prediction: "If they see this, they will reject me"
↓
Person risks disclosure to a safe listener
↓
Listener responds with acceptance, not disgust
↓
Prediction is falsified; the nervous system registers "seen AND safe"
↓
Repeated over time, the old belief loses its authority
MechanismExplanation
Prediction errorThe brain updates beliefs through experience contradicting them, not through argument. Secrecy prevents any contradicting experience.
Co-regulationA calm, safe person helps the nervous system move from threat (sympathetic/dorsal) toward safety (ventral). Shame is soothed in the presence of another.
Ending secrecy's loadConcealment is cognitively and physically costly (rumination, tension). Disclosure releases that load.
Separating self from actSaying "I did X" (guilt-language) replaces "I am X" (shame-language) and makes repair possible.
Belonging restoredShame threatens belonging; being known and still included restores it.

5.2 The Big Four revisited

Emotion (from earlier study)How confession addresses it
Shame ("I AM bad")Exposure met with acceptance; identity separated from act
Guilt ("I DID wrong")Named honestly; repair and forgiveness received
Fear ("danger IS")Feared exposure survived; safety re-learned
Condemnation ("permanently judged")Verdict replaced by Romans 8:1 spoken by a real voice

PART 6: Why Confession Breaks the Babylonian System

"Babylon" in Scripture is more than a city. It begins at Babel (Gen 11:4): "Let us make a name for ourselves." Its DNA is self-salvation through human achievement, image, and structure, the same project Kruger names when he describes the fallen mind's response to the I Am Nots. In Revelation 18 Babylon is a system of commerce, luxury, and control that even trades in human lives (v. 13), and the call is: "Come out of her, my people" (v. 4). What follows is a theological reading of that symbol applied to shame; other readings of Babylon exist (political, eschatological), and this one does not exclude them.

6.1 How Babylon runs on shame

Babylonian featureHow it uses shameHow confession dismantles it
Make a name for yourselfShame drives the frantic need to be someoneConfession gives up the self-made name and receives the given one
Image managementFig leaves, curated appearance, "fine, thanks"Confession is deliberate un-covering
Performance for acceptanceWorth is earned; failure must be hiddenConfession admits the ledger cannot be balanced by me and receives a gift
Fear-based controlLeaders or systems hold your secrets as leverageWhat is already in the light has no leverage
Isolation and rivalryEveryone hides, so everyone comparesOne honest person makes honesty possible for the next
Transactional religionForgiveness as a payment systemConfession as tool replaces confession as currency (Part 4.3)

6.2 The chain-breaking effect

A system built on hiding cannot survive a community where people actually tell the truth in safety. When one person confesses and is received, the fear that "no one could love the real me" is publicly disproved. That is why confession spreads freedom (James 5:16) and why entrenched shame-based systems resist it: it removes their currency.

6.3 The counterfeit: confession used as control

The same act can be used in reverse. In Babylonian settings confession can be demanded by a leader, collected as leverage, publicized to humiliate, or required as proof of loyalty. That is exploitation using the language of holiness (see the Exploitation and Disguised Control study). Signs: it is compulsory; the listener has power over you; what you share is later used against you; the response is scolding or exposure rather than acceptance; there is no path to restoration afterwards. True confession is voluntary, to a safe listener, and ends in mercy.

7.2b Fill-in section for Joshua James Roberts

Use these prompts with his actual teaching: (1) What does he say breaks shame? (2) Does he say confession is required, helpful, or a fruit? (3) What does he say about vulnerability toward people, and what warnings does he give? (4) Where does he agree with Kruger or Jesudian, and where does he differ? (5) Which specific statements did you find in tension? Write them here: ______________________

7.3 A synthesis: both/and, in order

The tension dissolves when we notice these are not competing causes but different links in one chain:

1. GROUND: Truth revealed (the Father's acceptance is already a fact in Christ)
↓
2. SAFETY: A safe person or community (God through people)
↓
3. PRACTICE: Voluntary, wise vulnerability and confession
↓
4. RECEPTION: Acceptance experienced; nervous system and belief update
↓
5. FRUIT: A freed heart that can love, confess again without fear, and receive others

Revelation without practice leaves the wound at the level of theory. Vulnerability without the revealed truth has nothing solid underneath it and can slide into a shame-driven need to be absolved by people. Kruger's emphasis supplies the ground; the vulnerability emphasis supplies the path by which ground becomes lived experience. Both point at the same Father.
